title: America Catches Car Fever
summary: In the 1890s, American tinkerers began building cars in sheds and bicycle shops. Two brothers won a race through the snow, a young engineer named Henry Ford built a car with no reverse gear, and a doctor, a mechanic and a bulldog wearing goggles drove all the way across the United States.

sections.heading: A Huge Country with Muddy Roads
paragraphs: In the early 1890s, the newest motor cars were rattling along the roads of Germany and France. In the United States, things looked very different. America was enormous, about 4,500 kilometres from coast to coast, and most of it was linked by railways, not good roads. Outside the cities, roads were mostly dirt tracks that turned into deep mud after rain and clouds of dust in summer. Farmers lived miles from the nearest town and travelled by horse and wagon. Most Americans had never seen a car.

Yet the country had some big advantages. It had plenty of iron, wood, oil and coal. It had busy machine shops, bicycle factories and a huge, growing population eager for new gadgets. Bicycles had become a craze in the 1890s, and bicycle makers already knew how to build light frames, chains, wire wheels and air-filled tires. Many of America's first car builders started out in bicycle shops.

In 1900 there were only about 8,000 cars registered in the whole United States, a tiny number for a country of about 76 million people. But in the space of roughly fifteen years, a group of tinkerers, mechanics and businessmen would turn the car from a strange toy into the start of a giant industry. This part tells how America caught car fever.

sections.heading: The Duryea Brothers of Springfield
paragraphs: Our story begins in Springfield, Massachusetts, with two brothers, Charles Duryea and his younger brother Frank. Charles, born in 1861, had worked in the bicycle business. Frank, born in 1869, was a skilled toolmaker and mechanic. In the early 1890s they set out to build a gasoline-powered carriage, fitting a small engine to a horse buggy in a Springfield workshop.

On 21 September 1893, the Duryea motor wagon made its first test run on Taylor Street in Springfield. It was not pretty, and it was not fast, but it moved under its own power. Many historians call it one of the first successful gasoline cars built in the United States. Other Americans had experimented earlier, and some may have run petrol vehicles a little before the Duryeas, so it is fairest to say the brothers were among the first rather than definitely the very first.

What really set the Duryeas apart is what came next. In 1895 they founded the Duryea Motor Wagon Company in Springfield, often described as the first American company formed to build and sell gasoline cars. By the end of 1896 it had sold 13 cars, all built to the same design, which made them some of the first automobiles ever sold in the United States. Thirteen cars sounds like nothing today, but it was a start: a business making cars to sell, not just one inventor's private machine.

Sadly, the brothers fell out. They argued over money and plans, including whether to move the business to Detroit, and they split up before 1900. For the rest of their long lives, Charles and Frank each told the story in a way that gave himself more of the credit. Many historians believe Frank did much of the hands-on engineering that made the cars work, while Charles was the promoter and organiser, but the quarrel means some details of who did what are still uncertain.

sections.heading: Racing Through the Snow: Chicago, Thanksgiving 1895
paragraphs: In 1895 a Chicago newspaper, the Chicago Times-Herald, decided to hold America's first big motor car contest. The paper offered 5,000 dollars in prizes to encourage the new industry, and it hoped the race would sell lots of newspapers too. Eighty-three vehicles were entered. But building a car that actually worked was much harder than filling in an entry form. The race was postponed once because so few cars were ready, and when the day finally came, only six turned up at the start line: four gasoline cars and two electric ones.

The race was held on Thanksgiving Day, 28 November 1895. It was a terrible day for driving. A snowstorm had hit Chicago, and the course, about 54 miles (87 kilometres) from Jackson Park on the city's south side north to Evanston and back, was covered in slush, snow and mud. Imagine standing in the cold at dawn, wrapped in a heavy coat, as the strange machines coughed, popped and slithered away from the start, while horse-drawn sleighs glided by much more easily.

Frank Duryea drove the Duryea brothers' car. It was not a smooth ride. He had to stop for repairs, including a visit to a blacksmith's forge to fix a broken part, and he took a wrong turn at one point. But his car had one great advantage: air-filled tires, which gripped the slushy roads better than solid ones. After 10 hours and 23 minutes, Frank crossed the finish line in first place. That is an average of only about 5 miles per hour over the whole day, about the speed of a brisk walk, but he had finished, which most entrants could not do.

Second place went to a German-built Benz entered by Oscar Mueller of Decatur, Illinois. Near the end, Mueller passed out from the cold, and the race umpire riding with him, a young Detroit engineer named Charles Brady King, took the controls and drove the car across the line. The other cars, including both electrics, did not finish.

The prizes were a bit confusing. The judges gave a gold medal to the electric car built by Morris and Salom, based mostly on separate tests of design and performance. But the Duryea won the 2,000 dollar first prize, and Mueller's Benz won 1,500 dollars. Newspapers across the country reported the race, and suddenly thousands of Americans were talking about horseless carriages. The race also helped to show that pneumatic tires were the way forward.

sections.heading: Henry Ford: From Farm Boy to Night-Time Tinkerer
paragraphs: One of the people who read about the new motor cars with great excitement was a young engineer in Detroit, Michigan, named Henry Ford. He was born on 30 July 1863 on his family's farm in Greenfield Township, near Dearborn, just outside Detroit. His father, William, was a farmer who had come from Ireland. His mother, Mary, died in 1876, when Henry was only about 12, a loss he felt deeply.

Henry did not love farm work, but he loved machines. When he was about 12, his father gave him a pocket watch, and he soon became known for taking watches apart and putting them back together. By 15 he was repairing watches for friends and neighbours. He went to a small one-room school until about the eighth grade and never went to high school.

In 1879, aged 16, Henry walked off to Detroit to become an apprentice machinist, learning to cut and shape metal parts. He returned home for a while, operated and repaired portable steam engines for farmers, and was hired by the Westinghouse company to service its steam engines in the area. In 1891 he took a job as an engineer at the Edison Illuminating Company, which ran one of Detroit's electric power stations. He did well, and by 1893 he was chief engineer.

His job had one useful feature: he was on call at the power station at odd hours, which left time for experiments. In a brick shed behind his rented home on Bagley Avenue in Detroit, Henry, helped by friends, spent his nights and spare hours building a gasoline engine and then a whole small vehicle around it. His wife, Clara, supported him so strongly that he later called her 'the Believer'.

On 4 June 1896, in the early hours of the morning, the machine was ready. Ford called it the Quadricycle, because it ran on four bicycle-style wire wheels. It had a two-cylinder engine of about 4 horsepower that drove the back wheels with a chain, a seat for the driver, a tiller instead of a steering wheel and a small fuel tank under the seat. It weighed about 500 pounds (about 230 kilograms). The gearbox had only two forward speeds, and there was no reverse gear at all: to back up, you had to get out and push.

According to a famous story, the finished Quadricycle was too wide to fit through the shed's door, and Ford had to knock out part of the brick wall to get it out. Whether every detail of that tale is true or not, the Quadricycle worked. Ford drove it around the dark streets of Detroit, and later that year he sold it for 200 dollars, using the money to keep building. Years later he bought it back for 60 dollars. The original Quadricycle is now displayed at The Henry Ford museum in Dearborn, Michigan.

Ford was not the first person to drive a car in Detroit: Charles Brady King, the same engineer who finished the Chicago race at the wheel of Mueller's Benz, drove his own motor car on Detroit's streets a few months earlier, in March 1896. In 1896 Ford also met his famous boss, Thomas Edison, at a company meeting. When Ford described his gasoline car, Edison encouraged him to keep going, and Ford never forgot it.

sections.heading: Two Failures and a Third Try
paragraphs: Building one car is not the same as running a car company. Ford found that out the hard way.

In August 1899, backed by a group of Detroit investors, Ford left the Edison company and became chief engineer of the new Detroit Automobile Company. It was a disaster. Ford kept trying to perfect his designs, and the few vehicles the company made were expensive and not very good. In January 1901 the company was dissolved.

Ford decided that racing would prove his skill and attract new investors. In October 1901 he drove a racing car he had built himself and beat Alexander Winton, one of America's best-known carmakers, in a race at Grosse Pointe, near Detroit. The win brought fresh backers, and in November 1901 the Henry Ford Company was formed. Yet within a few months Ford quarrelled with his investors and left. They brought in a skilled precision engineer, Henry Leland, and renamed the firm after the founder of Detroit, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac. The Cadillac company went on to great success without Ford.

Ford kept racing. He built an enormous, roaring racing car called the '999', and in October 1902 the daring cyclist-turned-driver Barney Oldfield drove it to victory, becoming one of America's first racing stars. The publicity helped once more.

On 16 June 1903, Ford and a new group of investors, led by a Detroit coal dealer named Alexander Malcomson, founded the Ford Motor Company with 28,000 dollars in cash. Among the partners were the brothers John and Horace Dodge, whose machine shop built much of the running gear for Ford's first car, the 1903 Ford Model A. The company started small, in a rented building, with a handful of workers putting together parts made by other firms. This time, it worked. The Ford Motor Company sold cars and made money from its first year, and it is still one of the world's biggest carmakers today.

sections.heading: Ransom Olds and the Curved Dash
paragraphs: While Ford was struggling, another Michigan carmaker had already shown that many people would buy a car if the price was right. Ransom Eli Olds was born on 3 June 1864 in Geneva, Ohio, and grew up working in his father's engine and machine shop in Lansing, Michigan. In August 1897 he founded the Olds Motor Vehicle Company in Lansing. Two years later a rich copper and timber businessman, Samuel L. Smith, put money into the firm, which became the Olds Motor Works and moved its main factory to Detroit.

Olds built several experimental models. Then, on 9 March 1901, the Detroit factory caught fire and was badly damaged. According to the often-told story, only one prototype was saved: a small, light runabout with a front that curved up like the toe of a sleigh. Whether or not it happened quite that way, the company put this little car into production, and it became famous as the Curved Dash Oldsmobile.

The Curved Dash was simple and cheap for its time. It sat two people, had a one-cylinder engine of about 5 horsepower under the seat, was steered with a tiller and could reach about 20 miles per hour (32 km/h). It cost 650 dollars, still a lot of money when a factory worker might earn roughly 400 to 500 dollars in a whole year, but far less than the big hand-built cars of the rich.

To make many cars quickly, Olds bought many parts, such as engines and gearboxes, from outside machine shops, and organised his factory so that cars were put together step by step from those parts. Historians often call this an early assembly line, although it was not the moving, conveyor-driven kind that Ford's team would build later: the cars mostly stood still while workers and parts came to them.

The results were dramatic. Olds built about 425 Curved Dash cars in 1901, roughly 2,000 to 2,500 in 1902, and several thousand a year by 1903 and 1904, making it the best-selling car in America and one of the first cars built in large numbers anywhere. In all, about 19,000 were made. The car even inspired a hit song, 'In My Merry Oldsmobile', in 1905. Olds himself left the company in 1904 after disagreements with the Smith family and started another firm, using his initials: REO.

sections.heading: The Patent That Claimed Every Car
paragraphs: As American carmakers multiplied, they ran into a strange legal roadblock. It came from a man who had never built and sold a single car: George B. Selden, a patent lawyer from Rochester, New York.

Back in 1879, Selden had filed a US patent application for a 'road engine', a carriage powered by a light, liquid-fuelled internal combustion engine based on an American engine design by George Brayton. A patent gives an inventor the right to stop others from using an invention for a set number of years, usually counted from the day it is granted. Selden cleverly kept his application waiting, making changes and amendments for sixteen years, while the car industry grew up around him. Only in November 1895 was US Patent 549,160 finally granted. Because the clock started then, his patent would last until 1912, and its wording was so broad that it seemed to cover almost any gasoline car.

In 1899 Selden sold the rights to a group of investors connected with the Electric Vehicle Company, who set out to make carmakers pay. In 1903 many of the leading companies formed the Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers. Its members agreed to pay a small fee on every car they sold, shared between the patent owners and the association, and in return they could advertise that their cars were 'licensed'.

Henry Ford refused to pay. His new company was turned down when it asked to join, and he decided to fight. The patent owners sued Ford and several other independent carmakers, and the legal battle lasted about eight years. To make sure buyers were not scared away, Ford promised in advertisements to protect any customer who might be sued. In 1909 a judge ruled in favour of Selden, and it looked as if Ford had lost.

Ford appealed. In January 1911 the appeals court decided that Selden's patent was valid, but only for cars using the Brayton-type engine that Selden had described. Almost every real car used an engine based on Nicolaus Otto's four-stroke design instead, so they did not infringe. The patent, which had only about a year left to run, became almost worthless overnight. Ford became a hero to many Americans as the little company that had beaten a big monopoly, and the case helped convince carmakers to share patents more freely with each other in the years that followed.

sections.heading: Coast to Coast: The Doctor, the Mechanic, the Dog and Alice
paragraphs: By 1903 cars could putter around a city, but could one cross the whole continent? Many people thought it was impossible. There were almost no paved roads between cities, no road signs, few bridges designed for cars and no filling stations. Then came a bet.

In May 1903, at the University Club in San Francisco, a 31-year-old doctor from Vermont named Horatio Nelson Jackson accepted a 50 dollar wager that he could cross the United States by car in less than 90 days. He had no car, very little driving experience and no maps. He hired a young mechanic and driver, Sewall K. Crocker, and bought a slightly used Winton touring car with a two-cylinder, 20-horsepower engine. He named it the Vermont, after his home state.

Jackson and Crocker set off from San Francisco on 23 May 1903. The trip was a long list of troubles. A tire burst early in the journey. They lost spare parts, money and even Jackson's glasses along the way. In Wyoming they went about 36 hours without food. When the car's wheel bearings broke, they made do with bearings borrowed from a farm mowing machine, and they spent days waiting for spare parts to arrive by train. Sometimes they used ropes and a block and tackle to haul the car out of mud or up steep slopes.

In Idaho, near the town of Caldwell, the travellers gained a third crew member: a young bulldog named Bud. Newspaper stories gave different accounts of how they got him, but in a letter to his wife Jackson said he had paid 15 dollars. The car had no roof and no windshield, and the dust bothered Bud's eyes, so Jackson gave him his own pair of driving goggles. Bud became a celebrity, and crowds came out to see the dog in goggles.

The Vermont rolled into New York City in the early hours of 26 July 1903, after 63 days, 12 hours and 30 minutes. Jackson won his bet, although the trip reportedly cost him thousands of dollars, far more than the 50 he won. They were the first people to cross the United States by car. A motorcyclist, George A. Wyman, had reached New York a few weeks earlier on a motorised bicycle, so Jackson's record is specifically for the automobile. In 1944 Jackson gave the Vermont to the Smithsonian Institution, and it is still kept at the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.

Six years later, another driver made a crossing in the opposite direction, and this time the driver was a woman. Alice Huyler Ramsey, a 22-year-old from Hackensack, New Jersey, left New York City on 9 June 1909 in a green Maxwell touring car. The Maxwell-Briscoe company sponsored the trip, partly as publicity: it wanted to show that its cars were easy and reliable enough for anyone, including women, to drive. Ramsey brought three passengers: two older sisters-in-law and a 19-year-old friend, Hermine Jahns. None of them could drive, so Alice did all of it herself.

The journey was about 3,800 miles (around 6,100 kilometres) long. Only a tiny fraction of the route, about 152 miles, was paved. Ramsey changed flat tires, cleaned spark plugs and coped with breakdowns, sometimes waiting in small towns while parts were fixed or sent. She steered the heavy car through mud, sand, swollen streams and mountain passes. With only rough maps, the group sometimes, according to Ramsey's own account, found their way by following telephone poles, because the lines with the most wires usually led to the next town.

On 7 August 1909, after 59 days, Alice Ramsey drove into San Francisco. She was the first woman to drive across the United States. Decades later she wrote a book about the trip, 'Veil, Duster, and Tire Iron' (1961), and in 2000 she became the first woman inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame.

Jackson's and Ramsey's journeys showed something important. Cars were no longer just toys for city streets; with enough grit, they could tie a whole continent together. But at the start of the 1900s, most cars were still too costly for ordinary families. Henry Ford had a bold idea about that. As he later put it, 'I will build a motor car for the great multitude'. He meant a car simple and cheap enough for a farmer, a factory worker or a shopkeeper to own, and the car he built to keep that promise would change the world.

deepDive: Who built America's first car? The honest answer is that it depends on your definition. Several inventors ran self-propelled vehicles in the United States before the Duryeas, including steam carriages, and a few people may have run small gasoline machines in the early 1890s. The Duryea brothers' 1893 test in Springfield is usually counted as one of the first successful American gasoline cars, and their 1895 company as the first American firm set up to build and sell them; by the end of 1896 it had sold 13 identical cars. Even within the family, credit was disputed: Charles and Frank spent decades disagreeing about who had done the real work. Detroit had its own priority question. Charles Brady King drove a motor car there in March 1896, about three months before Henry Ford's Quadricycle, which is a reminder that Ford's fame came from what he did later, not from being first. The Selden patent is a classic case study in how patent law can be used. By delaying his 1879 application for sixteen years with amendments, Selden made sure his patent was granted in 1895, just as the industry was taking off, so it would last until 1912. The 1911 appeals court decision did not declare the patent invalid; instead it ruled that it covered only cars with Brayton-type engines, while nearly all real cars used Otto-type four-stroke engines. Economic historians point out that the case changed industry behaviour: afterwards, American carmakers formed a cross-licensing arrangement in which members shared most patents with each other without fees, which lowered legal costs and may have sped up innovation. Numbers also help explain the boom. In 1900 there were only about 8,000 registered cars in the US, but the Curved Dash Oldsmobile showed that a light car costing 650 dollars could sell by the thousands, roughly 425 in 1901 and several thousand a year by 1903 and 1904. The idea that price, not just engineering, would decide the car's future set the stage for Ford's Model T.
funFact: Bud, the bulldog who rode across America with Horatio Nelson Jackson in 1903, wore his own pair of driving goggles to keep the dust out of his eyes.
